chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ali ibn Al-No'man, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Sadeer who said:

We were in the presence of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), so we mentioned what the people had done after their Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and their humiliating the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him). So a man from the people said, 'May Allah keep you well, so where was the honor of the Banu Hashim and what was their number?' So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'And as for those of Banu Hashim who remained, it was only Ja'far and Hamza who had passed away, and there remained with him two men who were weak, humble, new in the era of Islam: Abbas and Aqeel, and they were from the freed ones. By Allah! If Hamza and Ja'far had been present with them, they would not have achieved what they achieved. And if they had seen the two of them, they would not have damaged themselves.'

key_terms.الطُّلَقَاءِ: The freed ones (slaves who were freed)

ai.seo_question: Why were the Banu Hashim considered weak or few during the Prophet's time according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (as) clarifies that the perceived 'weakness' of Banu Hashim during the critical period was due to the early martyrdom of key warriors like Hamza and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, leaving only the relatively new converts Abbas and Aqeel. This historical context underscores that the political and military dynamics were not solely determined by the number of Hashemites but by the specific timing of their presence and sacrifice. The narration highlights the divine wisdom behind the timing of martyrdoms, suggesting that even if Hamza and Ja'far had survived, their distinct roles might have led to different, yet equally significant, outcomes in preserving the faith.

By Allah (azwj)! If Hamza (as) and Ja’far (as) were present among them, they would not have achieved what they achieved. And had they seen them (as) two, they would not have damaged themselves’.
